skill.name: Show a character through action and speech
skill.why: Telling 'she was angry' is flat. Showing it lets readers work it out.
skill.how: Don't name the feeling. Show what the character does and says instead.

steps.say: This is me before the cooking contest. Three lines about me. Only one lets you see me.

show.nudge: This just names the feeling. Can you see Mo do anything?
Now we know where I am. But can you see me do anything?

show.text: Mo chewed his sleeve and checked the oven nine times.

steps.ask: Tap the line where you can see Mo do something.
steps.win: Yes! Sleeve chewing and nine oven checks. You can see me do it. That's an action.

steps.say: Nobody said how I feel in that line. But you can still tell.

show.text: Mo chewed his sleeve and checked the oven nine times.

options.reason: Sleepy people don't check an oven nine times. Look at what Mo does.
Proud people stand tall. Mo is chewing his sleeve. Why would he?

steps.win: Yes! You worked it out. 'Mo was nervous' tells you. The action shows you. That's show, not tell.

steps.say: You can show a feeling with what someone says, too. Listen to me at the contest.

show.text: Mo was worried about the oven.
show.nudge: This names the feeling: worried. Which line lets Mo's own words show it?

show.text: 'It's fine. It's totally fine. Is it on fire?'

show.nudge: That's about the oven, not Mo. Which line has Mo talking?

steps.ask: Tap the line where Mo's words show the feeling.
steps.win: Yes! Nobody says nervous. But 'Is it on fire?' tells you everything. That's speech.

steps.say: Zed fixed 'Mo was nervous' for me. He wrote this. Is it showing now?

show.text: Mo was very, very, VERY nervous.

steps.ask: Is Zed's line showing or telling?

options.text: Showing. Very, very makes it bigger.
options.reason: Bigger isn't showing. Can you see Mo do anything?

options.text: Telling. It still names the feeling.
Showing. Nervous is a strong word.
options.reason: A strong feeling word is still a feeling word. What does Mo do or say?

steps.win: Right. A bigger feeling word is still telling. So is a new one, like terrified. Show what I do.

steps.say: Your go. Tully kicked the winning goal. My draft says 'Tully was proud.' Let's show it.
steps.ask: Which line shows that Tully is proud?

options.text: Tully felt very happy and proud.
options.reason: Two feeling words, but still telling. What would a proud Tully do or say?

options.text: Tully was super proud of her goal.
options.reason: Super proud still names the feeling. Show what she does or says.

options.text: Tully pointed at her name on her jumper. 'Did everyone see that?'

steps.win: Yes! An action and her own words. We never needed the word proud.

steps.say: Last trick. Writers often show a feeling, then tell it anyway. Find the extra bit.

show.nudge: Keep that! It shows the feeling. Find the part that names it.
Keep that too. His words show it. Find the part that names it.

steps.ask: Tap the part you could cut.
steps.win: Yes! Cut it. The door and the yelling already show it. Now cover the feeling words in your story.

terms.means: Names the feeling, like angry or nervous. Quick, but dull.
What the character does, like chewing a sleeve or slamming a door.
What the character says, in speech marks.

examples.text: Mo chewed his sleeve and checked the oven nine times.

card.test: Cover every feeling word. Can a reader still tell how the character feels?

weDo.frame: Mo is writing about the day Wren met a snake at the park.
weDo.prompt: Which sentence shows that Wren is brave?
weDo.hint: Which action would only a brave person do?
weDo.success: Stepping in front of a snake is brave, and her calm words prove it. You worked it out.

options.text: Wren stepped between the snake and the little kids and said, 'Everyone back up. Slowly.'
Wren grabbed the little kids and ran screaming all the way back to the car park.
options.reason: Running away screaming shows Wren is scared, not brave. What would a brave person do?

options.text: Wren felt brave and calm when she saw the snake sliding towards the little kids.
options.reason: Brave and calm are feeling words. This tells us how Wren feels instead of showing what she does.

weDo.frame: Mo is writing about Zed's game night. One line just names the feeling.
weDo.prompt: Tap the line that names a feeling. Then choose a line that shows it.
weDo.hint: Feeling words tell. What would Zed do with his hands?
weDo.success: Throwing the controller shows he's frustrated, and the word never appears. That's showing.

parts.tap: Zed lost the boss level for the tenth time.
parts.reason: This says what happened, not how Zed feels. Find the line with a feeling word.

parts.tap: Then he turned the TV off without a word.
parts.reason: That's already an action. Find the line that names the feeling.

options.text: He threw his controller onto the couch.
He felt so frustrated he wanted to scream.
options.reason: Frustrated is still a feeling word. Show what Zed does instead of naming it.
Grinning is an action, but it shows Zed is happy. He just lost for the tenth time.

creature.name: Tawnip
creature.blurb: A frogmouth that never tells you how it feels. Watch its feathers puff and its beak clack, and you'll know.

workshop.mentor: Nan didn't sit down once in the whole first quarter. She stood on her seat with a thermos in one hand and a sausage roll in the other, and every time the umpire blew the whistle, she pointed the sausage roll at him like a sword. 'Are you blind, mate? That was holding the ball!' A man in front turned round to complain. Nan gave him one look over her glasses. He turned back very quickly. At three-quarter time, she leaned over and whispered, 'If we lose, nobody tells your grandfather I cried.'
workshop.ask:
Write five sentences that show how a character feels, without naming it.
Stuck? Start with: 'Maxx stared at the crashed screen.'
Challenge: show two feelings at once.
checklist: I never used a feeling word (sad, angry, scared).
I can point to one thing my character does.
I can point to one thing my character says.
I found one 'and then' and cut or changed it.
